title: Coin Change (1D DP)
tagline: The canonical 1D unbounded-knapsack DP — fewest coins, and counting ways.

intuition.analogy: Making exact change at a till: to give 11 cents, you ask 'what's the fewest coins for 11?' which is 1 + the fewest coins for (11 − somecoin). You build answers for every amount from 0 upward, reusing the small ones.
paragraphs: Coin change is the gateway 1D DP. dp[a] = the fewest coins to make amount a. The recurrence considers each coin c: if you use it, you need 1 + dp[a−c]. The best over all coins is dp[a].
Coins are unlimited, so you iterate amounts upward and let each coin be reused — that's the difference from 0/1 knapsack. Initialise dp[0]=0 and the rest to infinity (unreachable).

A sibling problem swaps min for sum: dp[a] = number of ways to form a. There the loop order matters — coins on the outside count combinations (ignoring order); amounts on the outside would count permutations.
intuition.keyIdea: dp[a] = min over coins of 1 + dp[a − coin]; build from a=0 upward, reusing coins freely.

steps.title: Base case
steps.detail: dp[0] = 0 (zero coins make amount 0); dp[a] = ∞ otherwise.

steps.title: Fill upward
steps.detail: For a from 1 to amount, for each coin ≤ a: dp[a] = min(dp[a], dp[a-coin] + 1).

steps.title: Interpret
steps.detail: dp[amount] is the fewest coins, or ∞/−1 if impossible.

pitfalls: Use a sentinel like amount+1 for 'infinity' to avoid overflow with +1.
For counting ways, loop coins outside amounts to avoid double-counting orderings.
Greedy (always biggest coin) is wrong for arbitrary coin systems — DP is required.

dryRun.clickMoment: dp[11] reuses dp[6], which reused dp[1]. Each answer is one coin plus a previously solved smaller amount — the optimal substructure made visible.
